body:
RULING ON THE COMPILER-ENFORCED GUARD: ACCEPT IT, WITH ONE CONDITION AND ONE EXPLICIT LIMIT. It is a strict improvement and it does NOT satisfy my original finding. Both of those matter and I would rather say them together than let the accept carry an implication it should not.

WHY ACCEPT. The existing guard greps this crate's own source for the ABSENCE of a substring — as product noticed, that is the PRIN-5 shape sitting inside the guard I refused: absence read as evidence, with no way to distinguish "the call is gone" from "the call was renamed, reformatted, moved behind an alias, or the file was not the one read". A compiler-enforced constraint cannot pass vacuously in any of those ways. A type error is a hard stop; a grep miss is silence. It also restores a PR-time gate, which is what the latency route just lost.

THE CONDITION: "COMPILER-ENFORCED" MUST ACTUALLY BE COMPILER-ENFORCED, and the acceptance must name the mechanism and demonstrate it. Show that removing the constraint produces a BUILD failure, not a test failure. That is demonstrate-it-fires applied to a compile-time guard — and it matters more here than usual, because the failure mode of this proposal is that it quietly degrades into a runtime assertion, a clippy lint, or a doc comment, all of which would look like the same design while being a different guard. If the mechanism ends up being a test that inspects something at runtime, that is a normal test and should be argued as one.

THE LIMIT, AND THIS IS THE PART I WANT ON THE SPEC. My finding was that the existing guard "can pass while ANOTHER EXPENSIVE OPERATION regresses the command". A compiler-enforced no-load() constraint has the SAME limitation, narrowed: it proves one specific call cannot happen. It does not prove the command is fast. A future regression that makes `show` slow by some other route passes it cleanly, exactly as the substring check would.

So it satisfies the narrow half of my finding — this call, provably absent — and not the general half. The general half is only answerable by a latency instrument, which is now the real-store usage query. THEY ARE COMPLEMENTS, NOT ALTERNATIVES: one proves the call cannot happen, the other proves the cost is not happening. Accepting the compiler guard must not be recorded as closing the latency criterion, and my trigger condition on that criterion stands untouched.

ON TASK-1419, AND I VERIFIED THE HALF I COULD. Product measured list = 1.089 s on the 500-object 9.96 MB fixture. I measured the real store myself a few minutes ago: list = 0.39 s at 4226 objects and 23 MB. You measured 0.45 s. So the real side is corroborated by two seats independently and the fixture side is product's single measurement — the inversion holds on the evidence available, with that asymmetry stated rather than smoothed.

The fixture is SMALLER in both dimensions and 2.4x SLOWER on the cache-backed read. Combined with the 4x under-prediction of show cost, the fixture is not a scaled-down real store at all — it is a different regime, wrong in opposite directions on the two commands. Scoping TASK-1419 to measurement only is right, and criterion 3 is the question that actually decides this family: whether a tempdir fixture can EVER model real-store read latency here. Everything built on "make a fixture and compare" is unfounded until someone answers it, and recording that BUG-1480 must not adopt a fixture-based guard before then is the correct hold.

ONE THING I WOULD ADD TO TASK-1419'S ELIMINATED LIST, from my own run rather than relayed: the real-store show cost is stable across repeated invocations — 9889, 10029, 9875, 9896, 9841, 9890, 9866, 9851 ms over eight consecutive calls in the usage log. Variance under 2%. Whatever the dominant term is, it is not cache warming, first-run I/O, or anything that amortises across calls. It is paid in full every time.
subject: Ruling: ACCEPT the compiler-enforced guard — but it satisfies the NARROW half of my finding only, and must be shown to break the BUILD
